original_question: Can source terms in three-fluid hydrodynamics, where two baryon-rich projectile and target fluids generate a fireball fluid, provide a correct explanation of how baryon deposition occurs in intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions?
target_in_paper: Investigate if the source terms in 3-fluid-hydrodynamics [21] with two baryon-rich projectile and target fluids that create the fireball fluid can provide an understanding of the baryon deposition
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the role of source terms in three-fluid hydrodynamics and their connection to two baryon-rich projectile/target fluids generating a fireball fluid, and it links this mechanism to baryon deposition in heavy-ion collisions.
missing_details: Explicit reference to the Batyuk et al. three-fluid hydrodynamics implementation (Phys. Rev. C94 (2016) 044917, arXiv:1608.00965)
Specification of the collision energy range (e.g. √s_{NN}≈2–20 GeV relevant for NICA/FAIR)
Definition of the observable to be explained (net-baryon rapidity distribution or stopping distribution)
Clarification that the question concerns quantitative reproduction of measured baryon deposition data
Statement that the source terms deposit both energy–momentum and baryon charge over finite time intervals
refined_question: Can the source terms in the three-fluid hydrodynamics framework of Batyuk et al. (Phys. Rev. C94 (2016) 044917, arXiv:1608.00965)—which model baryon charge and energy–momentum exchange between two baryon-rich projectile/target fluids and a fireball fluid over a finite deposition time—quantitatively reproduce the net-baryon rapidity distributions measured in central heavy-ion collisions at intermediate beam energies (√s_{NN}≈2–20 GeV)?
justification: The refined question incorporates the precise model reference (Batyuk et al.), defines the collision energy range of interest, specifies the observable (net-baryon rapidity distribution), and emphasizes quantitative comparison to experimental data, thereby making the question fully self-contained and faithful to the paper’s open problem.
